questionText: During storm operations, a field tech receives two dispatch orders simultaneously: Site A has been dark (LVD operated, loads lost) for 20 minutes; Site B has 2 hours of battery remaining but its generator has not started. Priority is:

choices.text: Site B — preventing the outage is more important than recovering from one
Site A — restoring a dark site immediately is the top priority; site B has time and the battery is the safety margin for that time
Flip a coin — both are equal priority
Call the NOC for guidance, then wait

explanation: Triage order: dark sites first. Site A is already causing a network outage — every minute of darkness is real impact. Site B has 2 hours of margin — head to Site A now, NOC coordinates Site B coverage.

category: Cell Sites, Huts & Outside Plant Power
questionText: The three power domains at a typical macro cell site are:

choices.text: Shelter power (DC plant), tower/revenue loads, and environmental systems (LVD-shedable)

explanation: Site anatomy in power terms: the DC plant in the shelter, the revenue-generating radio loads on the tower, and environmental support loads that the LVD can shed.

category: Cell Sites, Huts & Outside Plant Power
questionText: Reserve time is maintained by:

choices.text: Periodic battery capacity testing, site load auditing, and generator test runs — all three must be current for reserve time to be valid
Running the plant controller at a lower voltage

explanation: Reserve time is the intersection of battery capacity (Ah tested), load (A measured), and generator reliability — all three degrade independently and must be tracked.

category: Cell Sites, Huts & Outside Plant Power
questionText: A 4-hour reserve site that reaches LVD after 45 minutes of utility outage indicates:

choices.text: The LVD threshold is set too high
Battery capacity has degraded to less than 20% of design — a high-priority finding for string replacement
Normal variation in reserve time estimates

explanation: 45 min / 4 hour design = ~19% capacity. This is a critical deficiency requiring immediate action, not a service note.
referenceBookSection: Module 16 — Cell Sites, Huts & Outside Plant Power

category: Cell Sites, Huts & Outside Plant Power
questionText: Before connecting a portable genset to a cell site, the non-negotiable first step is:

choices.text: Start the genset and let it warm up
Verify the utility disconnect is open — prevent backfeed that could injure utility line crews

explanation: Utility open = no backfeed risk. Always verify this independently even if an interlock is supposed to enforce it.

category: Cell Sites, Huts & Outside Plant Power
questionText: After clearing an alarm at the cell site, the field tech must:

choices.text: Only log it in the service record
Also confirm with the NOC that the alarm has cleared in the monitoring system — failure to close the loop results in a duplicate dispatch
Send an email to the NOC manager

explanation: NOC loop closure is a professional basic. The monitoring system may not auto-clear; the NOC team needs a technician confirmation to close the event.
referenceBookSection: Module 16 — Cell Sites, Huts & Outside Plant Power

category: Cell Sites, Huts & Outside Plant Power
questionText: During storm response, the dispatch priority for a site with 90 minutes of battery remaining and a failed generator is:

choices.text: Second tier: the site has margin while sites already dark are the first priority

explanation: Triage: dark sites first (already impacting the network), then sites with margin approaching exhaustion, then generator failures with buffer, then monitored stable sites.

category: Cell Sites, Huts & Outside Plant Power
questionText: RF thermal burn risk near cell site antennas is due to:

choices.text: Electrical shock from the antenna terminals
Radio frequency energy from transmitting antennas depositing heat in tissue at close range — real risk at cell site power levels
UV radiation from the tower lighting

explanation: RF at transmitter power levels creates localized tissue heating at close range to the antenna — the occupational safety concern for tower-proximity work.

category: Cell Sites, Huts & Outside Plant Power
questionText: For a DC power plant technician, the RF zone on a cell site typically is:

choices.text: Not in the shelter — DC power work is in the shelter; above-roof or antenna-proximity work requires RF safety awareness and clearance

explanation: DC plant work stays in the shelter. RF risk increases only if work takes the tech near or above the roofline to the antenna arrays — at which point RF status must be confirmed.
referenceBookSection: Module 16 — Cell Sites, Huts & Outside Plant Power

category: Cell Sites, Huts & Outside Plant Power
questionText: Cable voltage drop from shelter to tower equipment at high DC current is managed by:

choices.text: Using smaller gauge wire to reduce resistance
Sizing cable for the current and run length to keep voltage drop within equipment specifications — undersized cables steal effective bus voltage from loads
Running AC to the tower instead

explanation: Long DC cable runs at high current (100+ A) require careful conductor sizing; millivolt drops over 50–100 feet add up and reduce effective voltage at the equipment.

category: Cell Sites, Huts & Outside Plant Power
questionText: A site load audit is performed to:

choices.text: Confirm total DC load has not grown beyond the battery reserve-time design — new radio equipment adds load invisibly over time

explanation: Network equipment additions (LTE/5G upgrades, new RRH units) increase site load without triggering a formal design review — the load audit catches this drift before it shrinks reserve time silently.

subcategory: The Telecom Power Market and Your Role
questionText: Tower companies (American Tower, Crown Castle) differ from national carriers as employers because:

choices.text: They do not employ power technicians

They own the physical tower infrastructure and maintain the site power plant independent of the carrier tenants — their power tech role focuses on the infrastructure, not the carrier's network equipment
They only do solar power installations

explanation: Tower companies are neutral hosts to multiple carriers on one tower — they maintain the shared infrastructure (power, shelter, ground system) while carriers maintain their own radio equipment on the structure.

subcategory: The Telecom Power Market and Your Role
questionText: Storm response work is significant for telecom power techs because:

choices.text: It is overtime-compensated, often with hazard differentials, and represents a significant income multiplier for field techs deployed during disaster recovery
Carriers never pay overtime during storms

explanation: Storm deployment is premium-compensated work. Techs who build a reputation for reliable storm deployment are preferentially dispatched to high-value recovery missions.

subcategory: Certifications, Route Work, and Career Paths
questionText: A carrier's NEBS GR-1089 compliance requirement for a DC plant installation means:

choices.text: The equipment must be painted a specific color
All conductive elements must be bonded to the main ground bar per specified methods, documented and auditable — non-compliance is a rejected installation
NEBS only applies to radio equipment, not power plants

explanation: NEBS GR-1089 governs bonding and grounding comprehensively. Non-compliant installations fail carrier audits and must be corrected before acceptance — the compliance documentation is as important as the physical work.

subcategory: Certifications, Route Work, and Career Paths
questionText: The most valued field technician profile in modern carrier telecom power work is:

choices.text: A specialist in only DC plant rectifiers
Multi-discipline: DC plant, UPS, and generator in one resource — carriers prefer deploying one tech who can troubleshoot the full power chain
A NOC analyst who has never been on a site

explanation: Carriers minimize truck rolls and maximize site resolution rates by preferring techs who can diagnose and resolve any power element on the site. The portal's multi-course structure builds exactly this profile.

questionText: Tower companies (American Tower, Crown Castle) employ power technicians to:

choices.text: Maintain only the carrier's radio equipment
Maintain the shared site infrastructure — power plant, shelter, grounding, generator — independent of the carrier tenants

explanation: Tower companies are neutral infrastructure hosts. Their power tech role covers the shared plant that all carrier tenants depend on.

questionText: A route-based DC power tech typically maintains:

choices.text: 50–200 cell sites per territory with scheduled PMs and NOC-dispatched alarm response

explanation: Route work is the daily reality: a territory of sites, regular PM visits, and alarm-driven emergency response. Solo, truck-based, judgment-intensive.

questionText: Storm response work is financially significant for telecom power techs because:

choices.text: Carriers waive normal billing during storms
Overtime and hazard differentials during disaster events significantly supplement base compensation
It only lasts a few hours

explanation: Extended deployment during storms at overtime rates with hazard differentials can equal months of normal income in days — a meaningful career factor for mobile field techs.

questionText: Carrier-specific qualification programs (AT&T, Verizon, T-Mobile) are:

choices.text: In addition to foundational credentials — they authorize work on specific carrier platforms and equipment; the foundation translates across all of them

explanation: Platform qualifications layer on top of foundational knowledge. The foundation enables the tech to learn any platform faster; the platform training authorizes specific site work.

questionText: NEBS GR-1089 is most relevant to DC power techs because:

choices.text: It governs bonding and grounding requirements in carrier facilities — the same practices that prevent the millivolt-drop and return-path problems of field service
It only applies to new construction, not field service

explanation: Proper bonding and grounding per NEBS GR-1089 is the installation standard that field service must maintain and restore. Understanding it makes compliance audits understandable, not arbitrary.

questionText: The multi-discipline tech profile (DC plant + UPS + generator) is preferred by carriers because:

choices.text: One resource can troubleshoot and resolve any element of the site power chain — minimizing truck rolls, dispatch complexity, and site downtime

explanation: Multi-discipline capability directly translates to faster site resolution and fewer escalated dispatches. This is the carrier's operational preference and the field tech's career differentiator.

questionText: Jr. Telecom Power Technician entry compensation is approximately:
explanation: Jr. telecom power tech entry is $20–$30/hr, scaling to $35–$55/hr at senior level, with engineering and management paths above that.

questionText: The career path from field tech to power engineer typically requires:

choices.text: Accumulated field experience recognized by the carrier, or an EE/technical degree — the engineering role designs plant infrastructure rather than servicing it

explanation: Power engineer roles involve infrastructure design and carrier standards compliance — they require demonstrated technical depth beyond field service, typically via degree or extensive senior field experience.

questionText: The NOC operations analyst career path differs from field tech by:

choices.text: Moving from truck-based site response to office-based alarm management, dispatch coordination, and portfolio monitoring — off the road, higher complexity

explanation: NOC analyst roles leverage field experience for remote diagnosis and dispatch coordination. They are office-based, often regionally or nationally scoped, and represent a promotion track for techs who prefer operations to field work.

questionText: A telecom power tech's most distinctive daily tool compared to a generic field tech is:

choices.text: Mastery of the DC plant architecture, battery reserve-time management, and carrier-specific plant controller systems

explanation: DC plant architecture, reserve-time discipline, and plant controller literacy are what a telecom power specialist brings that a generic field tech does not. This course builds that distinctive knowledge base.
